items.title: JoltUI
items.text:
JoltUI is a small TypeScript framework for building single-page applications out of browser-native Web Components. Every building block (a button, a page, the layout around it) is a genuine custom element registered with the browser's Custom Elements API. There is no virtual DOM and no template compiler: components extend HTMLElement, render HTML strings into themselves and update only the parts of the page that change.

import { CustomElement, component, html, page, react } from "joltui";

@page({ path: "/", title: "Home" })
@component({ tagName: "home-page" })
export default class HomePage extends CustomElement {
    @react(0)
    accessor count!: number;

    override markup = () => html`
        <h1>Hello from JoltUI</h1>
        <p data-bind="count">Clicked {{= this.count }} times</p>
        <button type="button" @click="increment">Click me</button>
    `;

    increment(): void {
        this.count++;   // refreshes only the <p data-bind="count">
    }
}

items.title: What is included
items.text:
• Declarative decorators that turn classes into components, pages and layouts.
  • A router with typed route parameters, layouts, sublayout chains, and authentication and authorization.
  • doT-based templates with event binding, arguments and partial re-rendering through data-bind regions.
  • Reactive properties for component state, application data and query parameters.
  • Lifecycle hooks that run at well-defined moments.
  • Centralized error handling with handler classes and error chaining.
  • Cooperative cancellation: work that belongs to a removed component or a superseded navigation stops cleanly.
  • Lazy dependencies, server-rendered components and an opt-in template cache.
  • A Vite plugin that discovers pages at build time.

items.title: Inspired by Java
items.text:
JoltUI borrows its style from Spring, Jakarta EE and JAX-RS: annotations become decorators, exceptions are handled centrally, errors carry their cause, lifecycle callbacks are annotated methods, and the framework is extended by subclassing.

JoltUI Java analogue @component({ tagName }) Spring @Component @page({ path }) JAX-RS @Path, Spring @GetMapping @auth(["ADMIN"]) @RolesAllowed, @PreAuthorize ErrorHandler + @handles(E) @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler @lifecycle(BEFORE_INIT) @PostConstruct @lifecycle(AFTER_DISCONNECT) @PreDestroy error.cause Throwable.getCause() class MyApp extends App<MyApp> Enum<E extends Enum<E>>

JoltUI uses the standard TC39 decorators implemented by TypeScript 5, not the older experimentalDecorators.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: A JoltUI application builds to a static bundle: HTML, JavaScript chunks and assets. Any static web server or CDN can host it, as long as it sends unknown paths to index.html.

items.title: Build
items.text:
npx vite build

The output is written to dist/. Preview the production build locally with:

npx vite preview

items.title: The history-API fallback
items.text:
The router uses the History API, so URLs such as /posts/42 exist only in the browser. When a user reloads that page or opens a bookmark, the server receives a request for /posts/42 and must answer with index.html; the router then renders the right page. Without the fallback, the server returns its own 404.

nginxApacheCaddyNetlifyPython (Patera) 
server {
    listen 80;
    root /srv/my-app/dist;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
    }

    # Hashed assets can be cached forever.
    location /assets/ {
        add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
    }
}

# .htaccess in the dist/ folder
<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
    RewriteEngine On
    RewriteBase /
    RewriteRule ^index\.html$ - [L]
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
    RewriteRule . /index.html [L]
</IfModule>

example.com {
    root * /srv/my-app/dist
    try_files {path} /index.html
    file_server
}

# public/_redirects (copied to dist/ by Vite)
/*    /index.html   200

Serve dist/ as static files and add a catch-all route that returns index.html for paths that are not API endpoints. Keep API routes under a prefix such as /api, so the fallback never hides them.

Keep API paths out of the fallback

A fallback that answers everything with index.html turns a mistyped API call into an HTML response with status 200. Exclude your API prefix (and the server-components endpoint) from the fallback, so they return proper errors.

items.title: Hosting below a path
items.text:
To serve the application from a sub-path such as /portal/, configure both the build and the router:

vite.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
    base: "/portal/",
    plugins: [/* ... */],
});
src/app/app.ts
return new MyRouter({
    app: this,
    baseLayout: MainLayout,
    defaultTarget: "#page",
    baseUrl: "/portal",
});

base makes Vite emit asset URLs below /portal/; baseUrl prefixes every page path. Links in templates must contain the full path (/portal/about), or use router.redirect(path, { useBaseUrl: true }) for programmatic navigation. See Base URLs.

items.title: Checklist
items.text:
• Configure the history-API fallback and test a reload on a deep URL.
  • Exclude API paths from the fallback.
  • Cache hashed assets (/assets/*) for a long time; serve index.html with Cache-Control: no-cache so users pick up new releases.
  • Enforce authorization on the server. @auth only guards the user interface.
  • Escape untrusted data in templates with {{! }} (Templates), and consider a Content Security Policy.
  • Point serverComponentsUrl at the production endpoint, if you use server components. Requests include credentials, so the endpoint must be same-origin or configured for credentialed CORS.
  • Register an error handler for RouteNotFoundError, so unknown URLs show a proper page (Error pages).
  • Build with the same TypeScript settings as in development (standard decorators, useDefineForClassFields).

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
This section creates a new project, configures TypeScript and Vite, and builds a minimal application with one layout and two pages. The concepts behind each file are explained in the guide; here the aim is to get something on the screen.

  1. Installation: packages, TypeScript and Vite configuration.
  2. Quickstart: a layout, two pages, a router and the application.
  3. Project layout: where the files of a JoltUI application usually live.
  4. A first component: an interactive component with reactive state.

Already know Web Components?

A JoltUI component is a custom element. Everything you know about HTMLElement, the light DOM and global style sheets still applies. JoltUI uses no shadow DOM, so frameworks such as Bootstrap style components directly.

items.title: Command line tools
items.text:
The package exposes a joltui executable:

npx joltui init
npx joltui agents
npx joltui agents claude

npm exec -- joltui init is equivalent. npm joltui init is not an npm command. When using the scoped distribution, bootstrap with npx --package=@pro/joltui joltui init; configure your private registry first. The unqualified npx joltui works when the executable is installed locally, or when the package is published as joltui on your configured registry.

items.title: Create an application
items.text:
Run init in your application root, including after npm init and installing JoltUI. It scaffolds the current directory, without creating a nested project.

init asks for an application name (defaulting to the existing package name or directory name), whether to include Vite (yes), whether to include the JoltUI Vite plugin (yes when Vite is selected), and whether to install dependencies immediately (yes). The app name is used for application metadata, never as an output directory.

Existing package metadata, scripts, and dependency versions are preserved; missing scripts and dependencies are added to the same package.json. Installation runs in that directory and reuses its node_modules and lockfile. Existing README and ignore files are preserved. Conflicting source or configuration files stop initialization before any files are changed. In an empty directory, init creates package.json.

The starter includes TypeScript configuration, an HTML entry, an application, router, layout, reactive counter page, stylesheet, and npm scripts. Without the plugin, pages are registered explicitly. Without Vite, configure your own bundler before serving the app; npm run typecheck remains available.

npx joltui init my-app --yes
npx joltui init my-app --yes --no-install
npx joltui init my-app --yes --no-plugin
npx joltui init my-app --yes --no-vite

--yes accepts defaults and is required without an interactive terminal. --no-install writes files without running npm. Install failures retain the generated files so you can correct registry settings and rerun npm install. Existing scoped framework dependencies are reused directly. When adding dependencies, scoped releases generate npm aliases to their scoped framework and plugin packages.

items.title: Coding agents
items.text:
Run agents from your application root. The optional agent name is generic (default), codex, or claude, case insensitive.

  • Generic and Codex: AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/joltui/.
  • Claude: CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills/joltui/.

Existing instruction text is preserved and a JoltUI skill link is appended. The skill includes a topic index and the Markdown guides, getting-started material, and API references bundled with the installed framework version. Agents can read only the topics they need, including components, routing, reactivity, templates, lifecycle, authentication, errors, cancellation, caching, server components, and deployment.

An existing JoltUI skill directory is never overwritten. To refresh documentation after upgrading, move the old skill directory aside, then rerun the command.

items.title: A first component
items.text:
Components that are not pages are declared with @component alone. This counter keeps its state in a reactive property and re-renders only the paragraph that displays it:

src/app/components/counterButton.ts
import { CustomElement, component, html, react } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "../app.js";

@component({ tagName: "counter-button" })
export default class CounterButton extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    @react(0)
    accessor count!: number;

    override markup = () => html`
        <p data-bind="count">Clicked {{= this.count }} times</p>
        <button type="button" @click="increment">Click me</button>
    `;

    increment(): void {
        this.count++;
    }
}

To use it, import the module (importing is what registers the element) and write its tag in any template:

src/app/pages/homePage.ts
import "../components/counterButton.js";

// ...inside HomePage.markup
html`
    <h1>Hello from JoltUI</h1>
    <counter-button></counter-button>
`;

What happens:

  1. @click="increment" connects the button's click event to the increment method.
  2. Assigning this.count invalidates the count binding.
  3. JoltUI re-evaluates the template of the element marked data-bind="count", and only that element changes.

{{= ... }} is a doT expression evaluated with the component as this. Reactivity explains bindings in detail.

items.title: Passing arguments
items.text:
Attributes that start with : (short for data-jolt-) are the component's arguments:

<counter-button :label="Likes" :start="10"></counter-button>

override markup = () => html`
    <p data-bind="count">{{! this.args.label }}: {{= this.count }}</p>
    <button type="button" @click="increment">+1</button>
`;

Values are parsed as JSON when possible, so :start="10" arrives as the number 10.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• a modern browser with Custom Elements and the History API;
  • TypeScript 5 with standard decorators (the TC39 proposal, not experimentalDecorators);
  • an ES-module build tool. The documentation uses Vite.

items.title: Create the project
items.text:
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y
npm install joltui
npm install --save-dev typescript vite \
    vite-plugin-typescript-transform joltui-vite-plugin
  • joltui-vite-plugin discovers pages automatically (Vite plugin). It is optional; without it you list the pages on the router yourself.
  • vite-plugin-typescript-transform compiles TypeScript with the TypeScript compiler itself, so standard decorators and accessor fields are emitted exactly as TypeScript defines them.

items.title: TypeScript configuration
items.text:
The important options are the ES2022 target, useDefineForClassFields and the absence of experimentalDecorators:

tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "lib": ["ES2022", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
    "strict": true,
    "useDefineForClassFields": true,
    "experimentalDecorators": false,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts", "vite.config.ts"]
}

experimentalDecorators must be off

JoltUI's decorators follow the standard decorator signature. With experimentalDecorators: true, TypeScript emits the legacy form and the decorators fail.

items.title: Vite configuration
The HTML page
items.text:
JoltUI renders into a single container element. Everything else in index.html is ordinary HTML: style sheets, fonts, analytics and so on.

index.html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My App</title>
</head>
<body>
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.ts"></script>
</body>
</html>

Continue with the quickstart.

items.title: Project layout
items.text:
JoltUI does not prescribe a folder structure, but the following layout keeps the roles of the files obvious and matches the examples in this documentation:

my-app/
├── index.html
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
├── vite.config.ts
└── src/
    ├── main.ts                 creates the App and calls init()
    └── app/
        ├── app.ts              MyApp extends App<MyApp>
        ├── router.ts           MyRouter extends Router<MyApp>
        ├── errorHandler.ts     MyErrorHandler extends ErrorHandler<MyApp>
        ├── types.ts            shared types (User, Post, ...)
        ├── dependencies.ts     shared lazy() dependencies
        ├── layouts/
        │   └── mainLayout.ts
        ├── pages/
        │   ├── homePage.ts
        │   └── aboutPage.ts
        ├── components/
        │   └── counterButton.ts
        └── errorPages/
            └── notFoundPage.ts
File Role main.ts Entry point. The Vite plugin injects the page registry here. app.ts The application class: router, error handlers, app-level hooks. router.ts The router subclass: authentication checks and title generation. errorHandler.ts Error handlers. layouts/ Components decorated with @layout. pages/ Components decorated with @page, one per file, default-exported. components/ Ordinary components. errorPages/ Components shown with router.showErrorPage().

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• One page per module, as the default export. The Vite plugin requires it, and it makes the route table easy to read.
  • Type the application everywhere. Declare components as CustomElement<MyApp>, routers as Router<MyApp> and handlers as ErrorHandler<MyApp>. this.app is then typed as your own class.
  • Import components where they are used. Importing a module is what registers its custom element.
  • Use import type for the application class in components, to avoid circular runtime imports between app.ts and the modules it references.

items.title: The demo application
items.text:
The JoltUI repository contains Fieldnotes, a complete demo in dev/: a story list, article pages, a login, a protected drafts area and a profile section with a sublayout. Run it with:

npm install
npm run dev

items.title: Quickstart
items.text: This page builds an application with a layout, two pages, a router and the application class.

items.title: A layout
items.text:
A layout is the frame around your pages: header, navigation, footer. It contains an element that the router fills with the current page, here <main id="page">.

src/app/layouts/mainLayout.ts
import { CustomElement, component, html, layout } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "../app.js";

@layout
@component({ tagName: "main-layout" })
export default class MainLayout extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <header>
            <nav>
                <a href="/">Home</a>
                <a href="/about">About</a>
            </nav>
        </header>

        <main id="page"></main>

        <footer>Built with JoltUI</footer>
    `;
}

items.title: Pages
items.text:
A page is a component that the router renders for a URL.

src/app/pages/homePage.ts
import { CustomElement, component, html, page } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "../app.js";

@page({ path: "/", title: "Home" })
@component({ tagName: "home-page" })
export default class HomePage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <h1>Hello from JoltUI</h1>
        <p>This page is a custom element called <code><home-page></code>.</p>
    `;
}
src/app/pages/aboutPage.ts
import { CustomElement, component, html, page } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "../app.js";

@page({ path: "/about", title: "About" })
@component({ tagName: "about-page" })
export default class AboutPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <h1>About</h1>
        <p>Running on {{= this.app.appName }}.</p>
    `;
}

Decorator order matters

@component must be the decorator closest to the class. Decorators run bottom-up: @component registers the element and its metadata, and @page, @layout and @auth above it extend that metadata. Putting @page below @component throws @page requires @component to be applied below it.

items.title: Router and application
items.text:
The router knows the layout, the default target selector and (thanks to the Vite plugin) all pages. The application creates the router in its routerGenerator() method.

src/app/router.ts
import { Router } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "./app.js";

export default class MyRouter extends Router<MyApp> {}
src/app/app.ts
import { App } from "joltui";
import MainLayout from "./layouts/mainLayout.js";
import MyRouter from "./router.js";

export default class MyApp extends App<MyApp> {
    protected override routerGenerator(): MyRouter {
        return new MyRouter({
            app: this,
            baseLayout: MainLayout,
            defaultTarget: "#page",
        });
    }
}
Without the Vite plugin

List the pages on the router explicitly:

import AboutPage from "./pages/aboutPage.js";
import HomePage from "./pages/homePage.js";

const pages = [HomePage, AboutPage] as const;

return new MyRouter({
    app: this,
    pages,
    baseLayout: MainLayout,
    defaultTarget: "#page",
});

The entry point creates the application and initializes it in the container:

src/main.ts
import MyApp from "./app/app.js";

const app = new MyApp({
    appName: "My App",
    dataStructure: {
        user: null,
    },
});

await app.init("#app");

items.title: Run it
items.text:
npx vite

Opening http://localhost:5173/ shows the layout with the home page inside it. Clicking About changes the URL and swaps the page without reloading the document: same-origin links are intercepted by the router automatically.

items.title: Build for production
items.text:
npx vite build

The output in dist/ is a static bundle. Because the router uses the History API, the web server must answer unknown paths with index.html; see Deployment.

items.title: Conventions
items.text: Code is TypeScript and imports from the joltui package. Many examples refer to an application class called MyApp; its definition is on the Application page. Examples show only the code that matters for the point at hand.

items.title: Application
items.text: The App class is the root of every JoltUI application. You never use it directly: you extend it, configure it through its constructor and override the methods that customise it.

items.title: Defining the application class
Configuration
items.text:
The constructor takes an AppConfig object:

Option Default Meaning appName (required) Non-empty application name; also used by router.setTitle("_default"). dataStructure {} Declares the shared data fields and their initial values. serverComponentsUrl null Endpoint for server-rendered components. container null Container element, if not passed to init(). templatesCacheDuration 300 Default template-cache lifetime in seconds. templatesCacheCleanupInterval 60 Seconds between automatic cache cleanups; 0 disables them. src/main.ts
const app = new MyApp({
    appName: "Fieldnotes",
    dataStructure: {
        posts: [],
        user: null,
    },
    templatesCacheDuration: 180,
    serverComponentsUrl: "/api/components",
});

await app.init("#app");

init(target?) accepts a CSS selector or an element. It throws when neither target nor container identifies an existing element.

items.title: Shared application data
items.text:
dataStructure declares the fields of the application's shared state. Only declared fields can be read or written:

const posts = app.getData<Post[]>("posts");
app.setData("posts", [...posts, newPost]);

app.getData("unknown"); // Error: Data field 'unknown' does not exist.

Every setData() call dispatches an app-data-change event on the container, with the field name in event.detail.field. The event is dispatched even if the new value equals the old one. Components react to it in two ways:

  • regions marked data-bind="app.<field>" re-render (Reactivity);
  • components whose @component configuration names the field as dataField re-render completely.

You can also listen yourself:

import { dataEventEnum } from "joltui";

app.addEventListener(dataEventEnum.CHANGE, event => {
    console.log("changed:", event.detail.field);
});

Replace values instead of mutating them

setData stores whatever you give it. Mutating an array returned by getData changes the stored value but notifies nobody. Build a new value and pass it to setData.

Components have shortcuts for the same operations: this.getData(), this.setData() and the read-only this.data map.

items.title: Query parameters
items.text:
The App is the gateway to the URL's query string:

const page = app.queryParameters.page ?? "1";

queryParameters returns a plain Record<string, string>. Change parameters through the App, not through history directly, so that bound markup is notified:

// Merge: set or replace individual parameters; null removes one
app.updateQueryParameters({ page: 2, filter: "active" });
app.updateQueryParameters({ filter: null });

// Replace the entire query string
app.queryParameters = { page: "1", sort: "name" };
app.setQueryParameters({ page: "1", sort: "name" }); // same thing

Both forms compare the old and new parameters. If anything changed, they push a new history entry and dispatch one query-parameter-change event per changed parameter. Markup bound to query.<name> then refreshes.

createQueryParametersString(params, exclude?) builds an encoded query string, optionally leaving some keys out:

app.createQueryParametersString({ page: 2, q: "web components" });
// "page=2&q=web+components"

items.title: Lifecycle hooks on the App
Scoped DOM helpers
items.text:
Several DOM methods on the App operate on the container rather than the whole document, which keeps application code from reaching outside its own element:

Member Delegates to querySelector, querySelectorAll container.querySelector* getElementById(id) container.querySelector("#id") getElementsByClassName, getElementsByTagName the container matches(selector) container.matches children, childNodes the container insertAdjacentHTML the container addEventListener, removeEventListener the container

items.title: Other members
items.text:
Member Description router The router instance; throws if none was created. container The container element. appName The configured name. currentRouteParameters Parameters of the current route ({} before routing). generateHash(length = 16) Random hexadecimal string of length bytes (2 * length characters). pathname, hash, host, hostname, port, origin Shortcuts to location. handleError(error) Offers an error to the error handlers; rethrows if unhandled. handleErrorOnce(error) Same, but each error object is handled at most once. clearTemplatesCache() and related Template-cache management.

The complete member list is in the App reference.

items.title: Architecture
items.text: This page introduces the main building blocks, shows how they are wired together and follows an application from startup to the first rendered page.

items.title: The building blocks
items.text:
Part Role App The application object. Owns the container element, shared data, query parameters, the template cache, lifecycle hooks and the error handlers. Router Maps URLs to pages, renders layouts and pages into the container, checks authentication and handles navigation. CustomElement Base class of every component, layout and page. Renders templates, binds events, manages its lifetime and lifecycle. Layout A CustomElement decorated with @layout: the frame into which pages are rendered. Page A CustomElement decorated with @page: the component a route renders. ErrorHandler A class whose @handles(...) methods deal with errors raised anywhere in the application. Decorators @component, @page, @layout, @auth, @lifecycle, @handles, @react, @reactFactory, @queryParam, @select, @selectAll. lazy() Declares dynamically imported dependencies of a component. Vite plugin Build-time discovery of @page classes, so the router does not need a list of pages.

The App is created first. Its routerGenerator() method creates the Router, which renders the route's base layout, any sublayouts and the page into the app's container. Pages and layouts are ordinary components and can contain any number of further components. All of them extend CustomElement.

Two kinds of communication flow back up:

  • Components read and write shared state through the App (getData, setData, updateQueryParameters). The App answers with DOM events (app-data-change, query-parameter-change) that make components refresh the affected parts of their markup.
  • Errors raised in components, the router or server-component requests are passed to app.handleError(), which offers them to the registered ErrorHandler classes.

items.title: How components find the application
items.text:
There is no global singleton and no dependency injection. When app.init() runs, the App stores itself on the container element (container.app) and marks the container with an app-id attribute. When a component initializes, it looks up its nearest ancestor with that attribute:

const appContainer = this.closest("[app-id]");
this._app = appContainer.app;

From then on this.app is available in the component, typed as your own application class. A component outside the app container cannot initialize; it fails with "Failed to detect application container".

items.title: Startup sequence
items.text:
What happens, in order, when await app.init("#app") runs:

  1. Resolve the container. The argument can be a selector or an element. The App sets container.app and a random app-id.
  2. Start the template-cache cleanup timer (Template caching).
  3. Patch DOM prototypes (once per page; see below).
  4. Instantiate the error handlers listed in errorHandlers.
  5. Run @lifecycle(BEFORE_INIT) hooks on the App, then EXTENSION_INIT hooks.
  6. Create the router by calling routerGenerator(). The router registers a click listener on the container and a popstate listener on window.
  7. Route the current URL. The router matches location.pathname, authorizes it, renders the layout chain and the page, and waits until they have initialized.
  8. Wait for all top-level components in the container.
  9. Run @lifecycle(AFTER_INIT) hooks on the App.

When init() resolves, the first page is fully rendered.

items.title: The patched DOM
items.text:
At startup the App replaces a handful of DOM prototype members:

  • the innerHTML and outerHTML setters and insertAdjacentHTML;
  • setAttribute, getAttribute, removeAttribute, hasAttribute and toggleAttribute;
  • querySelector and querySelectorAll on both Document and Element.

The patches change behaviour only where JoltUI needs it:

  • HTML inserted inside a component is a template. If the target element belongs to a JoltUI component, innerHTML, outerHTML and insertAdjacentHTML run the string through the template engine with that component as this, expand the @event and :argument shorthands, and attach event listeners. Outside components the native behaviour is untouched.
  • :name attributes are shorthands for data-jolt-name. el.setAttribute(":mode", "dark") writes data-jolt-mode, and el.getAttribute(":mode") reads it back. On a component host, changing such an attribute also refreshes markup bound to attr.mode.
  • Selectors understand the shorthand too. querySelector("[:mode=dark]") is rewritten to [data-jolt-mode=dark]. JoltUI parses selectors with a bundled fork of css-what.

Because of these patches, ordinary DOM code inside a component behaves like JoltUI code. This inserts a row whose @click handler is bound to the component's removeItem method:

this.querySelector("#list")?.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", html`
    <li>{{! this.newItem }}
        <button @click="removeItem">×</button>
    </li>
`);

items.title: The rendering pipeline
items.text:
Whenever a component renders, it follows the same steps:

  1. Obtain the template string from markup(), from the server (useServer), from the template cache or, for prerendered components, from the existing child markup.
  2. Evaluate it with doT, using the component as this. While compiling, JoltUI records the raw template of every data-bind region.
  3. Expand shorthands: @click becomes jolt-click and :id becomes data-jolt-id.
  4. Insert the HTML and tag the new elements with data-parent-id (the component's hashId) and data-render-time.
  5. Hydrate: for every jolt-<event> attribute, add an event listener that calls the named method on the component.
  6. Child custom elements are upgraded by the browser and run their own initialization; the parent waits for them before it counts as initialized.

items.title: Data flow
items.text:
Shared state lives in the App. Components never subscribe to a store explicitly; the template declares which regions depend on which data:

<div data-bind="app.user">
    {{? this.app.getData("user") }} Signed in {{??}} Guest {{?}}
</div>

When code calls app.setData("user", u), the App dispatches an app-data-change event. Every component listens to it, looks up the regions bound to app.user and re-renders only those. The same mechanism serves query parameters (query.<name>), component attributes (attr.<name>) and component-local @react properties. See Reactivity.

items.title: Error flow
items.text:
Every place where JoltUI runs your code wraps it:

  • event handlers and lifecycle hooks (MethodExecutionError);
  • markup() (RenderError);
  • component initialization (ElementInitializationError);
  • link-click navigation (RouteFailedError);
  • route matching and authorization (RouteNotFoundError, AuthenticationError, AuthorizationError);
  • server component requests (NetworkError, InternalServerError and others).

The wrapped error goes to app.handleError(). Each registered ErrorHandler inspects the error and its cause chain and, if it has a matching @handles method, deals with it. If none does, the error is rethrown so that it surfaces in the console. See Error handling.

items.title: Navigation
items.text: A navigation starts from a link click, a call to router.redirect() or the browser's Back and Forward buttons. The router begins a new navigation, aborting any navigation still in progress. It then matches the path, authorizes the whole layout chain, publishes the route parameters, and renders or reuses the base layout, the sublayouts and finally the page. Every step checks the navigation's AbortSignal, so the latest navigation always wins. See Routing and Layouts.

items.title: What JoltUI does not do
items.text:
• There is no virtual DOM and no diffing. Updates re-evaluate a template and replace the contents of a bound region or the whole component.
  • There is no shadow DOM. Components render into their light DOM, so global style sheets apply directly.
  • There are no nested route definitions. One page handles one route; composition happens through layouts and sublayouts.
  • Element instances are not reusable after removal. A disconnected component has ended its lifetime (Cancellation).

items.title: Authentication and authorization
items.text: The @auth decorator declares which pages and layouts need a signed-in user, and which roles that user needs. The router enforces the declarations before it renders anything. How a user is authenticated is up to your application: you answer two questions in your router subclass.

items.title: Declaring requirements
items.text:
import { auth, component, CustomElement, page } from "joltui";

// any signed-in user
@auth()
@page({ path: "/drafts", title: "Drafts" })
@component({ tagName: "drafts-page" })
export default class DraftsPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {}

// signed-in user with the ADMIN role
@auth(["ADMIN"])
@page({ path: "/admin/users", title: "Users" })
@component({ tagName: "admin-users-page" })
export default class AdminUsersPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {}

@auth goes above @page or @layout. It may only decorate pages and layouts, not ordinary components. Roles are values of any type (strings, enum members, numbers); JoltUI passes them to your code unchanged.

items.title: Protecting layouts
items.text:
A protected layout acts as a gatekeeper for every route that uses it, as a page layout or as a sublayout:

@auth(["STAFF"])
@layout
@component({ tagName: "admin-layout" })
export default class AdminLayout extends CustomElement<MyApp> {}

@auth(["BILLING"])
@page({
    path: "/admin/invoices",
    subLayouts: [{ target: "#page", layout: AdminLayout }],
    target: "#admin-content",
})
@component({ tagName: "invoices-page" })
export default class InvoicesPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {}

items.title: Implementing the checks
items.text:
The router has two methods that throw NotImplementedError by default. An application that uses @auth must override them:

src/app/router.ts
import { Router } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "./app.js";
import type { User } from "./types.js";

export default class MyRouter extends Router<MyApp> {
    override isAuthenticated(): boolean {
        return this.app.getData<User | null>("user") !== null;
    }

    override checkUserRoles(roles: unknown[]): boolean {
        const user = this.app.getData<User | null>("user");
        return Boolean(user && roles.some(role => user.roles.includes(role)));
    }
}

Both methods may be asynchronous, for example to ask the server or refresh a token:

override async isAuthenticated(): Promise<boolean> {
    if (this.app.getData("user")) return true;
    const response = await fetch("/api/session", { credentials: "include" });
    const session: User | null = response.ok ? await response.json() : null;
    this.app.setData("user", session);
    return session !== null;
}

items.title: How a route is checked
items.text:
For each navigation the router collects the requirements of the route's authentication chain: the layout, then each sublayout, then the page.

  1. If any member requires authentication, isAuthenticated() is called once. If it returns false, the navigation fails with an AuthenticationError.
  2. Then, for each member that lists roles, checkUserRoles(roles) is called with that member's roles. If any call returns false, the navigation fails with an AuthorizationError.

Requirements are therefore cumulative. In the example above, a user needs STAFF (from the layout) and BILLING (from the page) to open /admin/invoices. Within a single call it is up to you whether one matching role is enough (some) or all are needed (every).

All checks run before anything is rendered, and they run on every navigation, even when the protected layout is already on screen and would be reused. Route parameters are published only after authorization succeeds.

items.title: Responding to failures
items.text:
Authentication and authorization failures go to the application's error handlers:

import {
    AuthenticationError,
    AuthorizationError,
    ErrorHandler,
    handles,
} from "joltui";
import ForbiddenPage from "./errorPages/forbiddenPage.js";

export default class MyErrorHandler extends ErrorHandler<MyApp> {
    @handles(AuthenticationError)
    async signIn(error: AuthenticationError): Promise<void> {
        const target = encodeURIComponent(error.path);
        await this.app.router.redirect(`/login?target=${target}`);
    }

    @handles(AuthorizationError)
    async forbidden(error: AuthorizationError): Promise<void> {
        await this.app.router.showErrorPage(ForbiddenPage, {
            error,
            title: "Access denied",
        });
    }
}

AuthenticationError.path is the path the user tried to open. AuthorizationError additionally carries the roles that were required.

After a successful login, the login page redirects back:

@queryParam("target", "/")
accessor target!: string;

login = async (event: Event): Promise<void> => {
    event.preventDefault();
    this.app.setData("user", await this.signInWithForm(event));
    await this.app.router.redirect(this.target);
};

The same two errors are raised when a server component request is answered with 401 or 403, so one pair of handlers covers both cases.

Client-side checks are about user experience, not security

They keep users away from screens they cannot use, but anyone can modify JavaScript running in their own browser. Every API the application calls must enforce the same rules on the server.

items.title: Signing out
items.text:
Signing out is a data change followed by navigation:

logout = async (): Promise<void> => {
    this.app.setData("user", null);
    this.app.clearTemplatesCache();   // if cached templates depend on the user
    await this.app.router.redirect("/");
};

Bindings on app.user, such as the layout's Sign in / Profile switch, update immediately.

items.title: Lifetime and cancellation
items.text: Single-page applications create and remove components constantly. A page that is still loading data when the user navigates away should stop its work, and must certainly not write its results into a page that no longer exists. JoltUI gives every component a lifetime expressed as a standard AbortSignal.

items.title: The lifetime signal
items.text:
Every CustomElement has a read-only abortSignal. It is aborted when the element is removed from the DOM (disconnectedCallback). The abort reason is an ElementDisconnectedError.

Pass the signal to anything that accepts one:

@lifecycle(Lifecycle.BEFORE_INIT)
async loadComments(): Promise<void> {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/posts/${this.postId}/comments`, {
        signal: this.abortSignal,
    });
    this.comments = await response.json();
}

document.addEventListener("keydown", this.onKey, {
    signal: this.abortSignal,   // listener removed with the component
});

Work that cannot be cancelled, such as a dynamic import or a library without signal support, simply finishes. After every such await, check the signal before producing side effects:

async loadDetails(): Promise<void> {
    const { renderChart } = await import("./chartLibrary.js");
    this.abortSignal.throwIfAborted();   // stop if we were removed meanwhile
    renderChart(this.querySelector("#chart"));
}

items.title: What JoltUI does on removal
items.text:
When a component is disconnected:

  • its abortSignal is aborted;
  • its pending initialization promises (initComplete, initElement()) reject with an ElementDisconnectedError;
  • it stops listening to application data and query-parameter changes;
  • event handlers that are still awaiting stop waiting;
  • an in-progress render is abandoned before it commits any markup;
  • AFTER_DISCONNECT hooks run, with the signal already aborted.

Cancellation is not an error. ElementDisconnectedError is never passed to the application's error handlers, even when it propagates through a parent's initialization or through the router. Successful initialization still resolves initComplete immediately before AFTER_INIT, and once fulfilled it is not changed by a later disconnection.

items.title: Recognising cancellation
items.text:
When you call initElement() or rerender() yourself, or catch errors around work tied to the signal, use isElementCancellation(error). It also detects a cancellation hidden in an error's cause chain:

import { isElementCancellation } from "joltui";

try {
    await this.rerender();
} catch (error) {
    if (isElementCancellation(error)) return;   // expected: we were removed
    throw error;
}

JoltUI's own event, lifecycle and routing paths already do this.

items.title: Overlapping renders
items.text:
If render() or rerender() is called while a previous render is still in progress (for instance an asynchronous markup() waiting for the network), the latest render wins:

  • superseded calls resolve quietly without committing markup or running the remaining hooks;
  • existing bindings stay active until the replacement markup is ready;
  • the component's lifetime is unaffected.

Synchronous binding refreshes (invalidate, data changes) do nothing once a component's lifetime has ended.

items.title: Combining signals
items.text:
Sometimes work should stop for two reasons: the component disappears, or a newer request replaces the current one. Search-as-you-type is the classic case. AbortSignal.any combines both:

private searchController: AbortController | null = null;

async search(event: Event): Promise<void> {
    this.searchController?.abort();
    this.searchController = new AbortController();

    const signal = AbortSignal.any([this.abortSignal, this.searchController.signal]);

    const query = (event.target as HTMLInputElement).value;
    try {
        const response = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal });
        this.results = await response.json();
    } catch (error) {
        if (signal.aborted) return;   // replaced or removed: not a failure
        throw error;
    }
}

items.title: Navigation and cancellation
items.text: Every navigation has its own AbortController. When a new navigation starts, the previous one is aborted and the layouts, sublayouts and page it had started creating are removed, which ends their lifetimes. Layouts from a navigation that has completed are left alone and can be reused.

items.title: Rules for element instances
items.text:
• A removed instance cannot be reused. Its lifetime has ended; create a new element instead.
  • Moving an element in the DOM ends its lifetime too, because moving triggers disconnectedCallback. Do not detach and re-insert components to preserve their state; keep the state in application data instead.
  • Do not tie shared cached work to one component's lifetime signal (Template caching); cancelling it would affect every waiting component.

items.title: Component communication
items.text: JoltUI's preferred way for components to cooperate is the most explicit one: one component obtains a reference to another and calls its method. The call is visible at the call site, typed, and easy to follow with "go to definition", the same style a Java developer uses when one object collaborates with another, rather than broadcasting events and hoping someone listens.

items.title: Child to parent
items.text:
Every component knows the component that rendered it: this.parent. Wrap it in a typed getter and call the parent's methods directly:

@component({ tagName: "post-card" })
export default class PostCard extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <article>
            <h3>{{! this.args.title }}</h3>
            <button @click="choose">Read</button>
        </article>
    `;

    private get list(): PostList {
        return this.parent as PostList;
    }

    choose(): void {
        this.list.openPost(this.args.id as number);
    }
}

@component({ tagName: "post-list" })
export default class PostList extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <div class="grid">
            {{~ this.posts :post }}
                <post-card :id="{{= post.id }}" :title="{{! post.title }}"></post-card>
            {{~}}
        </div>
    `;

    openPost(id: number): void {
        void this.app.router.redirect(`/posts/${id}`);
    }
}

parent is the nearest enclosing JoltUI component, even when plain HTML elements sit in between, and it is set for lazily loaded children too.

items.title: Parent to child
items.text:
For configuration, pass arguments on the child's tag. To make a child do something later, select it and call its method:

@select<SearchBox>("search-box", { required: true })
accessor searchBox!: SearchBox;

clearAll(): void {
    this.searchBox.reset();
}

items.title: Siblings and unrelated components
items.text:
Components that do not contain each other find one another through the application. app.querySelector() searches the whole app container:

// in product-tile
async addToCart(): Promise<void> {
    const cart = this.app.querySelector<CartSummary>("cart-summary");
    await cart?.initComplete;          // make sure it has finished initializing
    cart?.addItem(this.args.sku as string);
}

When the caller must reach a specific instance, for example a reusable form calling back into whichever page embedded it, pass the target's hashId as an argument:

// in LoginPage.markup
html`<login-form data-caller-id="${this.hashId}"></login-form>`;

// in LoginForm
get caller(): LoginPage {
    const id = this.getAttribute("data-caller-id");
    return this.app.querySelector(`[data-hash-id="${id}"]`) as LoginPage;
}

async login(event: Event): Promise<void> {
    await this.caller.login(event);
}

Give the methods meant for other components clear names and keep them public; together they form the component's API.

items.title: Shared state
items.text: Direct calls are for commands: "open this post", "add this item". When several components merely need to display the same state, keep it in application data and let bindings refresh each of them. No component then needs to know about the others.

items.title: DOM events
items.text:
DOM events still work and are useful in one situation: a generic, reusable component that must not know who uses it. An @event attribute on a child's tag binds to the parent's method:

// child: dispatch
this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("post-selected", {
    bubbles: true,
    detail: { id: this.args.id },
}));

<!-- parent template -->
<post-card :id="7" @post-selected="openPost"></post-card>

Within an application, prefer the explicit call: it shows at a glance which component depends on which.

items.title: Components
items.text: Everything visible in a JoltUI application is a component: a class that extends CustomElement and is registered with @component. Layouts and pages are components with extra metadata, so this page applies to them as well.

items.title: Declaring a component
items.text:
import { CustomElement, component, html } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "../app.js";

@component({ tagName: "user-card" })
export default class UserCard extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <article class="card">
            <h2>{{! this.args.name }}</h2>
            <p>{{! this.args.email }}</p>
        </article>
    `;
}

@component:

  1. validates the configuration;
  2. stores the component's metadata and sets the static tagName property;
  3. calls customElements.define(tagName, Class) when the class is defined.

The element is therefore registered as soon as its module is imported. Defining the same tag name twice with the same class is harmless; a tag name already registered with a different class throws.

items.title: Configuration options
items.text: Option Type Meaning tagName string Required. Lowercase, starting with a letter and containing at least one hyphen, e.g. user-card. dataField string Re-render the whole component when this application data field changes. useServer boolean Fetch markup from the server instead of calling markup() (Server components). groupName string Sent with server-component requests to group related components. cache boolean Cache this component's template (Template caching). cacheDuration number Cache lifetime in seconds; overrides the App default.

items.title: Where markup comes from
items.text:
A component gets its HTML from one of three sources, checked in this order:

  1. The server, if useServer: true. The response is used as the template.
  2. The markup method, if one is defined. This is by far the most common case.
  3. Its own children ("prerendered" markup). Without a server and a markup method, the component keeps the HTML it already contains, converts @event and :argument attributes to their long forms and attaches event listeners. Template expressions in it are not evaluated on this first pass.

Prerendered components are useful for progressive enhancement of HTML a server has already produced:

<!-- produced by the server -->
<newsletter-box>
    <form @submit="subscribe">
        <input name="email" type="email" required>
        <button>Subscribe</button>
    </form>
</newsletter-box>

@component({ tagName: "newsletter-box" })
export default class NewsletterBox extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    async subscribe(event: Event): Promise<void> {
        event.preventDefault();
        // ...
    }
}

Use prerendered markup sparingly

Child custom elements inside prerendered markup must already be registered when the host initializes. Import them, or declare them as lazy dependencies; otherwise initialization fails with an error naming the unregistered child. Heavy nesting of prerendered components is discouraged.

items.title: The markup method
items.text:
markup is a property holding a function that returns a template string, or a promise of one:

override markup = () => html`<p>Hello {{! this.args.name }}</p>`;

// Asynchronous markup: await data before producing the template
override markup = async () => {
    const response = await fetch("/api/stats", { signal: this.abortSignal });
    const stats: Stats = await response.json();
    return html`<p>${stats.visitors} visitors today</p>`;
};

items.title: The html helper
items.text: html is a tagged-template function that joins the literal parts and the interpolated values, turning null and undefined into empty strings. It exists so that editors highlight the HTML and build tools such as minify-html-literals can recognise and minify it.

items.title: ${...} versus {{= ... }}
items.text:
A template can contain two kinds of expressions, evaluated at different times:

  • ${expression} is JavaScript template-literal interpolation. It is evaluated when markup() runs, and its result becomes part of the template text.
  • {{= expression }} is a doT expression. It is evaluated when the template is rendered, and again every time a data-bind region containing it is refreshed.
override markup = () => html`
    <p>Rendered at ${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}</p>
    <p data-bind="count">Count: {{= this.count }}</p>
`;

Inside data-bind regions always use {{= }} or {{! }}

A ${} value is baked into the stored region template and never changes. The distinction also matters for the template cache, which stores the text after ${} and before {{ }} evaluation.

items.title: Using components inside components
items.text:
Import the module and write the tag:

import "./userCard.js";

override markup = () => html`
    <section>
        <user-card :name="Ada Lovelace" :email="ada@example.com"></user-card>
    </section>
`;

The parent waits until all of its direct child components have initialized before its own initialization completes. A layout is therefore ready only when everything inside it is ready.

items.title: Arguments
items.text:
Attributes that start with data-jolt-, or the shorthand :, are a component's arguments. this.args returns them as an object. Each value is parsed as JSON when possible, so numbers, booleans, arrays and objects arrive with their proper types:

<user-card :user-id="42" :admin="true" :tags='["staff","ops"]' :name="Ada"></user-card>

this.args; // { "user-id": 42, admin: true, tags: ["staff", "ops"], name: "Ada" }

Attribute names are case-insensitive

The HTML parser lowercases attribute names, so :userId arrives as this.args.userid. Use lowercase or kebab-case argument names.

items.title: Generating tags in code
items.text:
Every component class has a static generate(hashId?, args?) method that returns its tag as an HTML string, with arguments serialized and escaped:

import UserCard from "./userCard.js";

override markup = () => html`
    <ul>
        ${this.users.map(user =>
            `<li>${UserCard.generate(null, { "user-id": user.id, name: user.name })}</li>`,
        ).join("")}
    </ul>
`;

The router uses generate() itself to insert layouts and pages.

items.title: Events
items.text:
@click="save" means "when this element receives click, call this.save(event)". The long form jolt-click="save" is equivalent. Any event name works, including custom events with hyphens:

override markup = () => html`
    <form @submit="save">
        <input name="title" @input="validate">
        <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
`;

save = async (event: Event): Promise<void> => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget as HTMLFormElement);
    // ...
};

validate(event: Event): void {
    // ...
}

Handlers can be methods or arrow-function properties. They may be asynchronous; JoltUI awaits them and stops waiting if the component is removed in the meantime.

Do not reuse HTMLElement member names

A component is an HTMLElement. A handler called remove, click, focus, append or close, or a property called title, hidden or dir, replaces the element's own member. The router, for example, calls element.remove() to discard superseded pages. Choose specific names such as deletePost or closeDialog. The same applies to CustomElement's own members: app, args, data, cache, parent, metadata, render, rerender, invalidate and the others in the reference.

items.title: Handler arguments
items.text:
If the element that triggered the event has arguments, they are passed as a second parameter. This is the idiomatic way to tell list items apart:

override markup = () => html`
    <ul>
        {{~ this.posts :post }}
            <li>
                {{! post.title }}
                <button @click="deletePost" :post-id="{{= post.id }}">Delete</button>
            </li>
        {{~}}
    </ul>
`;

deletePost(event: Event, args: { "post-id": number }): void {
    const posts = this.app.getData<Post[]>("posts");
    this.app.setData("posts", posts.filter(post => post.id !== args["post-id"]));
}

items.title: Errors in handlers
items.text: If a handler throws or rejects, JoltUI wraps the error in a MethodExecutionError (with the original as cause) and passes it to the application's error handlers. You do not need try/catch in every handler just to report failures.

items.title: Re-rendering
items.text:
Three ways to update what a component shows, from most to least targeted:

  1. Bindings. A change to bound data refreshes only the bound regions. @react properties, app.setData, query-parameter updates and attribute changes do this automatically; this.invalidate("name") does it manually (Reactivity).
  2. dataField. A component configured with dataField: "user" re-renders completely whenever app.setData("user", ...) is called.
  3. rerender(). Re-renders the whole component on demand, running the BEFORE_RERENDER and AFTER_RERENDER hooks.
@component({ tagName: "account-menu", dataField: "user" })
export default class AccountMenu extends CustomElement<MyApp> { /* ... */ }

A full re-render replaces all of the component's children. Child components are recreated and lose their internal state, which is why bindings are usually the better tool. If several re-renders overlap, only the latest one is committed.

items.title: Selecting elements
items.text:
@select and @selectAll expose descendants as read-only accessor properties. The query runs every time the property is read, so it always reflects the current DOM:

import { select, selectAll } from "joltui";

@select<HTMLInputElement>("#email", { required: true })
accessor emailInput!: HTMLInputElement;

@select<HTMLElement>(".error")
accessor errorBox!: HTMLElement | null;

@selectAll<HTMLInputElement>("input[required]")
accessor requiredInputs!: NodeListOf<HTMLInputElement>;

validate(): boolean {
    return Array.from(this.requiredInputs).every(input => input.value);
}

With required: true, reading the property throws if nothing matches. Assigning to a selected property throws as well. Selectors may use the : shorthand: @select("[:role=primary]") matches data-jolt-role="primary".

items.title: Element identity
items.text:
Member Description hashId / data-hash-id Random identifier, unique per instance. data-parent-id hashId of the component that rendered this element. parent The parent CustomElement, if any. app The application instance. args Parsed arguments. metadata Decorator metadata (kind, tag name, configuration). initComplete Promise resolved when initialization succeeds. initializationState "pending", "fulfilled" or "rejected". initializationError The failure, if initialization was rejected. abortSignal Aborted when the element is removed (Cancellation). lastRender Timestamp of the last render.

The hashId makes it possible to find a specific instance; see Component communication.

items.title: Error handling
items.text: JoltUI routes errors from every part of an application to one place: the error handler classes registered on the App. The design follows the Java pattern of @ControllerAdvice classes with @ExceptionHandler methods: handlers are declared by annotating methods with the error types they handle, and the framework picks the right one.

items.title: Writing an error handler
Where errors come from
items.text:
You rarely call the error handlers yourself. JoltUI calls them for:

Source Error passed to the handlers An event handler throws MethodExecutionError (cause: your error) A lifecycle hook throws during initialization ElementInitializationError → MethodExecutionError → your error markup() throws during initialization ElementInitializationError → RenderError → your error A route does not exist RouteNotFoundError Authentication / authorization fails AuthenticationError / AuthorizationError A link-click navigation throws RouteFailedError (cause: the failure) A server component cannot be loaded see Server components

To report an error from your own code, pass it to the App:

try {
    await this.save();
} catch (error) {
    await this.app.handleError(error);
}

handleError throws if no handler accepts the error. handleErrorOnce remembers each error object and handles it only once; JoltUI uses it so that an initialization failure that propagates through several parent components is reported a single time.

items.title: Errors and their causes
items.text:
JoltUI wraps errors to add context: which method of which component failed. The original error is kept in the standard cause property, just like Java's exception chaining:

class ValidationError extends Error {
    constructor(readonly fieldErrors: Record<string, string>) {
        super("Validation failed");
        this.name = "ValidationError";
    }
}

// in a component
save(): void {
    throw new ValidationError({ title: "Title is required" });
}

The handlers receive a MethodExecutionError whose cause is the ValidationError. Handler resolution looks through the chain, so @handles(ValidationError) is called with the ValidationError itself.

items.title: How a handler is chosen
items.text:
For each error, the App asks its handler classes in registration order. The first class with a matching method handles the error, and the search stops. Within one class:

  1. Take the error.
  2. Exact type match: look for a method registered for the error's own class; if there is none, for its parent class, grandparent, and so on up to Error.
  3. instanceof match: otherwise, test the registered types with instanceof in discovery order. This includes types with a custom Symbol.hasInstance, which lets you handle errors from libraries such as Zod (@handles(ZodError)) without JoltUI depending on them.
  4. Follow the cause: otherwise, repeat with error.cause.

Discovery order is subclass methods before base-class methods, declaration order within a class, and argument order within @handles.

Keep catch-all handlers in a separate class

Step 2 walks up to Error. A @handles(Error) method therefore matches the outer wrapper, such as MethodExecutionError, before the cause is ever inspected. Put specific handlers in one class and a catch-all in a second class registered last:

override readonly errorHandlers = [
    MyErrorHandler,        // specific types, inspects causes
    FallbackErrorHandler,  // @handles(Error): logs and notifies
];

If no class handles an error, it is rethrown and appears in the browser console as an uncaught error. Nothing is swallowed silently.

items.title: Inheritance between handler classes
items.text:
• a decorated override in a subclass replaces the base method's registration;
  • an undecorated override removes it (decorators are not inherited);
  • unrelated inherited handlers stay active.

Two different effective methods in one class hierarchy cannot register the same error type; the constructor throws.

items.title: Error pages
items.text:
router.showErrorPage() renders any component as an error page without changing the URL or the history:

@handles(RouteNotFoundError)
async notFound(error: RouteNotFoundError): Promise<void> {
    await this.app.router.showErrorPage(NotFoundPage, {
        error,
        title: "Page not found",
    });
}

The error page is an ordinary @component. It does not need @page and is not registered with the router:

@component({ tagName: "not-found-page" })
export default class NotFoundPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <section class="not-found">
            <h1>404</h1>
            <p>Nothing was found at <code>{{! this.app.pathname }}</code>.</p>
            <a href="/">Back to the start</a>
        </section>
    `;
}
Option Default Meaning error — The error being handled; see below. title — Document title (passed through titleGenerator). layout base layout Layout to render the page in. target default target Target selector inside the layout. args — Arguments passed to the error page component.

While an error page is shown, router.currentRoute is null, route parameters are empty and the sublayout chain is removed. The normal route start, layout-change and finish events still apply. Error pages do not run authorization, so choose a layout that unauthenticated visitors may see.

Always pass the error

The router remembers which navigation produced the error. If the user has started a newer navigation by the time a slow handler calls showErrorPage, the call is ignored instead of replacing the newer page. A new navigation also cancels an error page that is still initializing, and showing a second error page while one is initializing is rejected, which prevents endless loops when the error page itself fails.

items.title: Initialization errors
items.text:
When a component fails to initialize, its initComplete promise rejects with an ElementInitializationError:

Property Description element The component instance that failed. elementName Its tag name. cause The underlying error (dependency, hook, render or child failure).

The same error object propagates unchanged to parent components waiting for the child, and the error handlers see it once.

The complete list of error classes is in the error reference.

items.title: Layouts and sublayouts
items.text: A layout is a component that frames pages: it renders the parts of the screen that stay the same between pages and contains a target element into which the router inserts the current page. JoltUI supports one base layout per route plus an optional chain of sublayouts between the layout and the page.

items.title: Declaring a layout
items.text:
A layout is a component with @layout above @component:

import { CustomElement, component, html, layout } from "joltui";
import type MyApp from "../app.js";

@layout
@component({ tagName: "main-layout" })
export default class MainLayout extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <header class="site-header">…</header>
        <main id="page"></main>
        <footer class="site-footer">…</footer>
    `;
}

Layouts are full components: they can have reactive state, bindings, event handlers and lifecycle hooks. Navigation menus, notification badges and sign-in status usually live in the layout.

items.title: The base layout and per-page layouts
items.text:
The router's baseLayout is used for every page that does not choose another one. A page can select a different layout, and a different target inside it:

@page({
    path: "/login",
    title: "Sign in",
    layout: AuthLayout,
    target: "#auth-content",
})
@component({ tagName: "login-page" })
export default class LoginPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> { /* … */ }

@layout
@component({ tagName: "auth-layout" })
export default class AuthLayout extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <main class="auth-shell">
            <a class="brand" href="/">MyApp</a>
            <div id="auth-content"></div>
        </main>
    `;
}

items.title: Layout reuse
items.text: When the next route uses the same layout class as the current one, the router keeps the existing layout instance and only replaces the page inside its target. The layout is not re-rendered: its state, scroll position and any open menus survive navigation. When the layout class differs, the router replaces the whole contents of the app container with the new layout and emits route-change.layout-change.finished.

items.title: Sublayout chains
items.text:
Larger applications often have sections with their own navigation, such as an account area with a sidebar or an admin area with tabs. Sublayouts express that nesting without nested route definitions:

@page({
    path: "/account/profile",
    title: "Profile",
    subLayouts: [
        { target: "#page", layout: AccountLayout },
        { target: "#account-content", layout: ProfileLayout },
    ],
    target: "#profile-content",
})
@component({ tagName: "profile-page" })
export default class ProfilePage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {}

The chain is resolved from the outside in:

  1. #page is looked up inside the base layout, and AccountLayout is rendered there;
  2. #account-content is looked up inside AccountLayout, and ProfileLayout is rendered there;
  3. the page's own target, #profile-content, is looked up inside the last sublayout, and the page is rendered there.

Every class in the chain must use @layout. Its module registers it through @component, and the router validates that registration from the page metadata.

main-layout                 (base layout)
└─ #page
   └─ account-layout        (sublayout 0)
      └─ #account-content
         └─ profile-layout  (sublayout 1)
            └─ #profile-content
               └─ profile-page

items.title: Reuse along the chain
items.text:
Sublayouts are reused the same way layouts are. When consecutive pages request the same ordered sequence of (target, layout) pairs, the existing sublayout instances and their state are kept. At the first difference, that sublayout and everything below it are replaced. A page without sublayouts removes the active chain before it renders.

@auth()
@layout
@component({ tagName: "profile-sublayout" })
export default class ProfileSublayout extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    override markup = () => html`
        <div class="row">
            <nav class="col-3">
                <a href="/profile">Profile</a>
                <a href="/profile-billing">Billing</a>
            </nav>
            <div id="subcontent" class="col-9"></div>
        </div>
    `;
}

@page({
    path: "/profile",
    title: "Profile",
    subLayouts: [{ target: "#page-content", layout: ProfileSublayout }],
    target: "#subcontent",
})
@component({ tagName: "profile-page" })
export default class ProfilePage extends CustomElement<MyApp> { /* … */ }

@page({
    path: "/profile-billing",
    title: "Billing",
    subLayouts: [{ target: "#page-content", layout: ProfileSublayout }],
    target: "#subcontent",
})
@component({ tagName: "profile-billing" })
export default class ProfileBilling extends CustomElement<MyApp> { /* … */ }

Moving between /profile and /profile-billing swaps only the contents of #subcontent; the sidebar instance stays in place. Navigating to /, a page without sublayouts, removes it.

To avoid repeating the chain on every page, keep it in a constant:

export const profileSection = [
    { target: "#page-content", layout: ProfileSublayout },
] as const;

@page({ path: "/profile", subLayouts: profileSection, target: "#subcontent" })

One page per route

JoltUI renders one page per route and has no nested route definitions. Sublayouts are the composition mechanism.

items.title: Targets
items.text:
Targets are CSS selectors. The router first checks whether the layout element itself matches the selector, then searches inside it. Use ids or other selectors unique within the layout; the first match wins.

Sublayout elements receive two extra attributes, data-jolt-router-layout and data-jolt-layout-depth (0 for the first sublayout), which are handy for styling and debugging.

items.title: Protecting a whole section
items.text: Because ProfileSublayout carries @auth(), every route that uses it requires a signed-in user. The pages themselves do not need the decorator. See Authentication.

items.title: Lazy dependencies
items.text: Large applications should not download everything up front. A component can declare lazy dependencies: modules imported on demand, right before the component initializes. Bundlers such as Vite turn each dynamic import() into a separate chunk, so the code is fetched only when a component that needs it actually appears.

items.title: Declaring dependencies
items.text:
Dependencies are listed in a static dependencies array, created with lazy():

import { CustomElement, component, html, lazy, page } from "joltui";

@page({ path: "/login", title: "Sign in", layout: AuthLayout })
@component({ tagName: "login-page" })
export default class LoginPage extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    static override readonly dependencies = [
        lazy(() => import("../components/loginForm.js"), "login-form"),
    ] as const;

    override markup = () => html`
        <section class="login-panel">
            <h1>Welcome back</h1>
            <login-form data-caller-id="${this.hashId}"></login-form>
        </section>
    `;
}

Before running its BEFORE_INIT hooks, the component loads all of its dependencies in parallel and waits for them. By the time the template renders, importing loginForm.js has registered <login-form>, and the tag upgrades immediately.

lazy(loader, name?) Meaning loader A function returning a promise, normally () => import("…"). name Optional label used in error messages.

items.title: Behaviour
items.text:
• Loaded once. A lazy() object remembers its pending or completed load. Every component that declares the same object shares one download.
  • Retried after failure. If loading fails, the cached promise is discarded and the next attempt tries again. The failure is reported as a DependencyLoadError with the original error as cause and the given dependencyName, and the component's initialization fails with it.
  • Inherited. Dependencies declared on base classes are loaded too, and an object declared at several levels is loaded only once.
  • Cancellable wait. If the component is removed while its dependencies load, it stops waiting. The download itself completes and stays cached for the next component.

items.title: Sharing and preloading
items.text:
To share a dependency between components, define it once in a module:

src/app/dependencies.ts
import { lazy } from "joltui";

export const chartWidget = lazy(
    () => import("./components/chartWidget.js"),
    "chart-widget",
);

import { chartWidget } from "../dependencies.js";

@component({ tagName: "sales-report" })
export default class SalesReport extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    static override readonly dependencies = [chartWidget] as const;
}

preload() starts the download ahead of time, for instance when the user hovers over a link that leads to a page needing the chart:

<a href="/reports/sales" @mouseenter="warmUp">Sales report</a>

warmUp(): void {
    void chartWidget.preload();
}

items.title: Prerendered markup needs registered children
items.text:
A component without markup adopts the HTML it already contains (Components). If that HTML contains custom elements, they must be registered before the host initializes. Declaring the child module as a lazy dependency solves this without a static import:

@component({ tagName: "product-gallery" })
export default class ProductGallery extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    static override readonly dependencies = [
        lazy(() => import("./productTile.js"), "product-tile"),
    ] as const;
}

items.title: Lazy dependencies and the Vite plugin
items.text: The Vite plugin imports every page statically, so page modules are part of the main bundle. Their lazy dependencies are still separate chunks. A good structure is therefore: lightweight page classes that declare their heavier components and libraries as lazy dependencies.

items.title: Lifecycle hooks
items.text:
Components and the application pass through well-defined stages. Methods decorated with @lifecycle(...) run at those stages, in the spirit of Java's @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy.

import { Lifecycle, lifecycle } from "joltui";

@lifecycle(Lifecycle.BEFORE_INIT)
async loadData(): Promise<void> {
    // runs before the first render
}

items.title: The stages
items.text: Stage App Component When BEFORE_INIT ✓ ✓ Before rendering (component) / before the router is created (App). EXTENSION_INIT ✓ Right after the App's BEFORE_INIT. BEFORE_INIT_RESOLVE ✓ After rendering and after all child components have initialized, before initComplete resolves. AFTER_INIT ✓ ✓ After initialization has completed. BEFORE_RERENDER ✓ At the start of rerender(). AFTER_RERENDER ✓ After rerender() and its children have finished. AFTER_DISCONNECT ✓ After the element has been removed from the DOM.

items.title: A component's initialization
items.text:
When a component is connected to the document, it:

  1. locates the App and assigns its hashId and parent;
  2. loads its lazy dependencies;
  3. runs BEFORE_INIT hooks;
  4. subscribes to data and query-parameter changes;
  5. renders its markup and attaches event listeners;
  6. waits until its direct child components have initialized;
  7. runs BEFORE_INIT_RESOLVE hooks;
  8. resolves initComplete;
  9. runs AFTER_INIT hooks.

Each hook is awaited before the next step starts, and every step checks that the element is still connected. If it has been removed, initialization stops quietly (Cancellation).

items.title: Typical uses
items.text:
BEFORE_INIT: load what the template needs. The template is rendered right after this hook:

@component({ tagName: "author-profile" })
export default class AuthorProfile extends CustomElement<MyApp> {
    private author: Author | null = null;

    @lifecycle(Lifecycle.BEFORE_INIT)
    async loadAuthor(): Promise<void> {
        const response = await fetch(`/api/authors/${this.args.id}`, {
            signal: this.abortSignal,
        });
        this.author = response.ok ? await response.json() : null;
    }

    override markup = () => html`
        <h2>{{! this.author?.name ?? "Unknown author" }}</h2>
        <p>{{! this.author?.bio ?? "" }}</p>
    `;
}

BEFORE_INIT_RESOLVE: work that needs the finished subtree. Child components have rendered, but the parent's initComplete has not yet resolved, so anything waiting on the parent also waits for this hook. Measure the DOM, set initial focus or initialise a third-party widget that must be ready before the page counts as loaded.

AFTER_INIT: start ongoing activity such as timers, polling and analytics:

private timer: number | undefined;

@lifecycle(Lifecycle.AFTER_INIT)
startClock(): void {
    this.timer = window.setInterval(() => this.invalidate("clock"), 1000);
}

@lifecycle(Lifecycle.AFTER_DISCONNECT)
stopClock(): void {
    window.clearInterval(this.timer);
}

AFTER_RERENDER: restore what a full re-render destroyed, for example re-initialising a widget attached to elements that have just been replaced.

AFTER_DISCONNECT: release resources. The element's abortSignal has already been aborted when this hook runs. Listeners registered with { signal: this.abortSignal } are removed automatically, so the hook is needed only for resources that do not understand abort signals:

@lifecycle(Lifecycle.AFTER_INIT)
watchResize(): void {
    // removed automatically when the element is disconnected
    window.addEventListener("resize", () => this.invalidate("size"), {
        signal: this.abortSignal,
    });
}

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• @lifecycle decorates methods. It cannot decorate static, private (#name) or symbol-named methods, nor arrow-function properties.
  • One method may subscribe to several stages: @lifecycle(Lifecycle.AFTER_INIT, Lifecycle.AFTER_RERENDER).
  • Several methods may subscribe to the same stage. They run one after another: base-class methods first, then subclass methods, each class in declaration order.
  • Overriding replaces registration. If a subclass overrides a decorated method, only the subclass's version counts. An undecorated override removes the hook; decorators are not inherited by overrides.
  • Hooks may be async; each is awaited before the next runs.

items.title: Failures
items.text:
An error thrown by a hook is wrapped in a MethodExecutionError that names the method and component and keeps the original error as its cause.

  • During initialization stages (BEFORE_INIT, BEFORE_INIT_RESOLVE), the failure is wrapped once more in an ElementInitializationError. initComplete rejects with it, initializationState becomes "rejected", and the application's error handlers process it once, even when it also propagates through parent components.
  • An AFTER_INIT failure is reported to the error handlers, but initComplete has already resolved and stays resolved.
  • Rerender failures are reported to the error handlers, and the promise returned by rerender() rejects.

items.title: Waiting for a component
items.text:
const card = this.querySelector<UserCard>("user-card");
await card?.initComplete;

For synchronous inspection, use initializationState ("pending", "fulfilled" or "rejected") and initializationError.

items.title: Reactivity
